lessons.title: Combining structures with invariants
lessons.summary: Choose one structure for each required operation.
lessons.body:
Most "design a data structure" problems share one idea: **no single structure gives you every operation cheaply, so you glue two together**. Each structure covers the other's weakness, and the hard part is keeping them in sync.

Here n is the number of stored items. Big-O describes how work grows with n, ignoring constant factors: O(1) stays bounded as the structure grows, while O(n) can grow in proportion to its size.

A hash map offers expected O(1) lookup but does not automatically maintain sorted-key or access-recency order. Python dictionaries do preserve insertion order. A linked list keeps order and can splice in O(1), but finding a node is O(n). An array gives O(1) access by position, but deleting from the middle is O(n). Combine them and you can often get O(1) for everything.

The method:

1. List the operations and the cost each must have.
2. For each operation, ask what it needs: lookup by key, an ordering, access by position?
3. Pick a structure for each need, and decide what the hash map's values point at (a node, an index).
4. Write down the **invariants** that tie them together, and check every operation preserves them.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A cloakroom register
> A cloakroom keeps both a ticket register and an ordered rail of coats.
>
> **How it maps:** The register finds a coat by ticket, while the rail keeps an ordering. Removing a coat requires updating both records, just as a composite structure must keep its map and list in agreement.
>
> **Where it stops:** A physical rail does not provide constant-time pointer changes; the comparison explains agreement between representations, not their running times.

These complexity claims assume constant-time key hashing/equality and word-sized values. Hash operations are expected amortised O(1), and dynamic-array append/pop can resize; these are not worst-case per-operation guarantees.

## Key takeaways

- Choose one structure for each required operation.
- Write down the invariant joining the structures before implementing updates.

## Further reading
- [CPython’s LRU cache implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.14.0/Lib/functools.py)
- [Python ordered dictionaries](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html)
- [Redis cache eviction policies](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/)

questions.prompt: A cache stores keys in both a hash map and a recency list. Eviction removes the list node but leaves its map entry. What invariant has failed?

options.text: A cached key must appear in both structures or neither.
options.explanation: Correct: the map now refers to a key that is absent from the live recency list.

options.text: Every key must have the same hash.
options.explanation: Equal hashes are neither required nor desirable for lookup.

options.text: The list must be sorted by key.
options.explanation: Recency order tracks accesses, rather than numeric or lexical key order.

options.text: Every get must scan all nodes.
options.explanation: A key-to-node map exists precisely to avoid scanning.

lessons.title: LRU caches and recency pointers
lessons.summary: A key-to-node lookup reaches the matching recency-list node.
lessons.body:
## LRU cache: hash map + doubly linked list

An LRU (least recently used) cache holds at most `cap` items. `get(key)` returns a value and marks it as recently used; `put(key, value)` inserts or updates, evicting the least recently used item when full. Both must be O(1).

- Lookup by key needs a hash map.
- Ordering by recency, with "move to front" and "remove oldest", needs a list we can splice in O(1).

So the map stores `key -> node`, and the nodes form a doubly linked list ordered from most to least recent.

```
map: {A: *, B: *, C: *}
            |     |     |
head <-> [B] <-> [A] <-> [C] <-> tail
 MRU                              LRU
```

Why doubly linked? To unlink a node you must update its predecessor's `next`. With only `next` pointers, finding the predecessor is O(n), where n is the number of nodes in the list, because you must walk from the head. The `prev` pointer makes removal O(1).

Why store the key in the node? When you evict the tail you must also delete it from the map, and the node is all you have.

```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key=None, val=None):
        self.key, self.val = key, val
        self.prev = self.next = None

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, cap):
        self.cap = cap   # assume cap >= 1
        self.map = {}    # key -> Node
        self.head = Node()  # MRU sentinel
        self.tail = Node()  # LRU sentinel
        self.head.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev = self.head

    def _unlink(self, n):
        # Bypass n in both neighbouring
        # links.
        n.prev.next = n.next
        n.next.prev = n.prev

    def _push_front(self, n):
        # Insert just after the MRU
        # sentinel.
        first = self.head.next
        n.prev, n.next = self.head, first
        first.prev = n
        self.head.next = n

    def get(self, key):
        n = self.map.get(key)
        if n is None:
            return -1
        self._unlink(n)
        self._push_front(n)
        return n.val

    def put(self, key, val):
        n = self.map.get(key)
        if n is not None:
            n.val = val
            self._unlink(n)
        else:
            if len(self.map) == self.cap:
                # Evict the oldest real
                # node, not tail.
                lru = self.tail.prev
                self._unlink(lru)
                # Remove the evicted key
                # from lookup too.
                del self.map[lru.key]
            n = Node(key, val)
            self.map[key] = n
        self._push_front(n)
```

> [!tip] Sentinel nodes
> The dummy `head` and `tail` nodes mean every real node always has a real `prev` and `next`. That removes every "is this the first node?" special case, which is where most hand-written linked-list bugs live.

The invariant: **a key is in the map if and only if its node is in the list**, and list order is recency order. Every branch of `put` maintains it: an update moves an existing node, an insert adds to both, an eviction removes from both.

In practice you rarely write this by hand. Python's `OrderedDict` (with `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)`) and Java's `LinkedHashMap` (with `accessOrder = true` and an overridden `removeEldestEntry`) are exactly this structure. CPython's positive, bounded `functools.lru_cache` uses a dict plus a circular doubly linked list; the unbounded mode does not need recency eviction.

## Key takeaways

- A key-to-node lookup reaches the matching recency-list node.
- Unlink and relink on hits; eviction removes a node from both structures.

## Further reading
- [CPython’s LRU cache implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.14.0/Lib/functools.py)
- [Python ordered dictionaries](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html)
- [Redis cache eviction policies](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/)

questions.prompt: An LRU cache uses a hash map from key to node plus a linked list ordered by recency. With no auxiliary predecessor map, why should the list be doubly linked for `get` to be O(1)?

options.text: So the list can be traversed from either end when searching for a key
options.explanation: Searching is the map's job, not the list's. The list is never searched; the map hands you the node directly.

options.text: Because unlinking a node needs its predecessor, and a `prev` pointer finds it in O(1)
options.explanation: Correct. Moving a node to the front means unlinking it first, which updates the predecessor's `next`. With a singly linked list, finding the predecessor is an O(n) walk from the head, where n is the number of nodes in the list.

options.text: Because a doubly linked list uses less memory per node
options.explanation: It uses more: one extra pointer per node. The extra memory is the price paid for O(1) unlinking.

options.text: So the most recently used item can be found at the tail
options.explanation: Either end can be designated MRU in any linked list; that is a convention, not a reason for the second pointer.

questions.workedExample:
1. `get(k)`: the map gives you node `n` in O(1).
2. You must now move `n` to the front. Step one is unlinking it:
```python
n.prev.next = n.next
n.next.prev = n.prev
```
3. Both lines need `n.prev`. In a singly linked list you would have to walk from the head until `p.next is n` (here `n` is the node). For a list of m nodes that walk takes up to m steps: O(m).
4. Storing `prev` in every node turns that walk into a pointer read, so the whole `get` is O(1).

questions.prompt: In the hand-written LRU cache, each node stores its `key` as well as its `val`. When is the key in the node actually used?

options.text: When `get` looks a key up
options.explanation: `get` looks the key up in the hash map, which already has the key; the node's copy is not needed there.

options.text: When updating an existing key's value in `put`
options.explanation: An update reaches the node through the map using the key passed in, so the stored key is not needed.

options.text: When evicting: the tail node is all you have, and you need its key to delete it from the map
options.explanation: Correct. Eviction starts from the list (`self.tail.prev`), not from a key. Without the key stored in the node you could not remove the matching map entry, and the map and list would drift apart.

options.text: Never; it is only there for debugging
options.explanation: Remove it and eviction cannot clean up the map, so evicted keys would still be found by `get`.

questions.workedExample:
Walk through each operation and ask where it starts:

| Operation | Starts from | Needs node.key? |
|---|---|---|
| get | key (map) | no |
| put update | key (map) | no |
| put evict | tail (list) | yes |

Eviction is the only path that begins at the list. It must do `del self.map[lru.key]`, so the key has to live in the node.

questions.prompt:
Using the lesson's `LRUCache` with capacity 2, what do the `get` calls return?

```python
c = LRUCache(2)
# Insert or refresh this cache entry.
c.put(1, 1); c.put(2, 2)
# Read and update cache metadata.
c.get(1)
# Insert or refresh this cache entry.
c.put(3, 3)
# Read and update cache metadata.
c.get(2)
# Insert or refresh this cache entry.
c.put(4, 4)
# Read and update cache metadata.
c.get(1); c.get(3); c.get(4)
```

options.explanation: This ignores eviction altogether; with capacity 2 the cache can never hold four keys.
Correct. `get(1)` makes 1 most recent, so `put(3)` evicts 2. Then 1 is the least recent when `put(4)` arrives, so 1 is evicted too.
This has `put(4)` evicting 3 instead of 1. After `put(3)` the order is `[3, 1]`, and the miss on 2 does not refresh 1, so 1 is the least recent.
This evicts 1 on `put(3)`, which is FIFO behaviour. LRU evicts 2, because `get(1)` made 1 more recent than 2.

questions.workedExample:
List MRU (left) to LRU (right):
```
put 1    [1]
put 2    [2, 1]
get 1 -> 1     [1, 2]
put 3    full, evict 2
         [3, 1]
get 2 -> -1    (miss, no change)
put 4    full, evict 1
         [4, 3]
get 1 -> -1
get 3 -> 3     [3, 4]
get 4 -> 4     [4, 3]
```
A miss does not change the order, so after `put(3)` key 1 stays at the LRU end and is the next victim.

questions.prompt: Which of these changes to the lesson's `LRUCache` would make it return **wrong results** (not merely run slower)? Select all that apply.

options.text: On eviction, unlinking the tail node but forgetting `del self.map[lru.key]`
options.explanation: Correct, this breaks it. `get` on the evicted key still finds its orphaned node and returns a stale value, and the map grows past capacity, so after the first eviction the `==` check never fires again and the cache grows without bound.

options.text: In `put`, updating an existing key's value without moving its node to the front
options.explanation: Correct, this breaks it. A write counts as a use in LRU. Leaving the node in place means a just-written key can be evicted next, the wrong victim.

options.text: Replacing the sentinel nodes with `None` checks for the head and tail, done carefully
options.explanation: Not a correctness change. Sentinels only remove special cases; careful `None` handling gives the same behaviour with more code.

options.text: In `put`, checking `len(self.map) == self.cap` and evicting before checking whether the key already exists
options.explanation: Correct, this breaks it. Updating an existing key in a full cache must never evict anything, but this order evicts the LRU item unnecessarily whenever it is a different key.

options.text: Using a singly linked list and finding each node's predecessor by walking from the head
options.explanation: This is slower (O(n) per access, where n is the number of cached items) but still correct, so it is not in the answer.

questions.workedExample:
Ask of each change: does the map still match the list, and is the list still in recency order?
1. Missing `del map[...]`: map has a key the list doesn't. Broken.
2. No move on update: list order is no longer recency order. Broken.
3. `None` checks instead of sentinels: same behaviour, different code. Fine.
4. Evict-before-lookup: cache with `{A, B}`, cap 2, B least recent, `put(A, new)` evicts B for no reason. Broken.
5. Singly linked list: same behaviour, O(n) cost. Fine but slow.

lessons.title: LFU caches and frequency buckets
lessons.summary: Move an accessed key exactly one frequency bucket upwards.
lessons.body:
## LFU cache: hash map + buckets of lists

An LFU (least frequently used) cache evicts the key with the fewest accesses, breaking ties by evicting the least recently used of those. Again, `get` and `put` should be O(1).

An indexed min-heap could put the least-used key at the top, but a hit changes its count and may require O(log n) work to restore heap order, where n is the number of cached keys. A key-to-heap-position map would also be needed to locate the entry quickly.

The constant-time trick is that **a frequency only ever goes up by one**. Keep a bucket for each frequency:

- `val`: key to value.
- `freq`: key to its access count.
- `by_f`: count to an ordered set of keys with that count, oldest first.
- `min_f`: the smallest count currently present.

```
min_f = 1
by_f[1]: D -> E       (D older)
by_f[2]: B
by_f[5]: A -> C
evict: oldest in by_f[min_f] = D
```

When a touched key leaves the lowest bucket empty, the next bucket becomes the minimum: the touched key has just entered it. A new key starts at count one and resets `min_f` to one. Neither operation needs to search for the next occupied bucket.

Worked example, using the bucket picture above: touch D, whose count f is 1. D moves to bucket 2, but bucket 1 still holds E, so `min_f` stays 1. Now touch E: bucket 1 empties and `min_f` was 1, so `min_f` becomes 2, and bucket 2 is guaranteed non-empty because E has just landed in it. No smaller bucket can be non-empty, because `min_f` was the smallest. The rules rely on counts only rising by one at a time; a design that could decrement or reset counts would need a real search.

```python
from collections import defaultdict
from collections import OrderedDict

class LFUCache:
    def __init__(self, cap):
        self.cap = cap  # assume cap >= 0
        self.val = {}   # key -> value
        self.freq = {}  # key -> use count
        # count -> keys, oldest first
        self.by_f = defaultdict(OrderedDict)
        self.min_f = 0

    def _bump(self, key):
        # Move only this key to the next
        # count.
        f = self.freq[key]
        del self.by_f[f][key]
        if not self.by_f[f]:
            del self.by_f[f]
            if self.min_f == f:
                # The moved key fills the
                # next bucket.
                self.min_f = f + 1
        self.freq[key] = f + 1
        self.by_f[f + 1][key] = None

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.val:
            return -1
        self._bump(key)
        return self.val[key]

    def put(self, key, value):
        if self.cap == 0:
            return
        if key in self.val:
            self.val[key] = value
            self._bump(key)
            return
        if len(self.val) == self.cap:
            g = self.by_f[self.min_f]
            # Oldest key breaks equal-count
            # ties.
            old, _ = g.popitem(last=False)
            if not g:
                del self.by_f[self.min_f]
            del self.val[old]
            del self.freq[old]
        self.val[key] = value
        self.freq[key] = 1
        self.by_f[1][key] = None
        self.min_f = 1
```

> [!warning] Evict before you insert
> In `put`, evict first and only then add the new key. If you insert first, `min_f` becomes 1 and the new key may be the only member of bucket 1. Evicting "the oldest key in the minimum bucket" then throws away the key you just added, while a stale key with count 2 survives.

Production caches seldom use exact LFU. Counts never decay in this design, so a formerly popular key can linger long after its usefulness ends. Redis uses an approximate, decaying 8-bit counter instead, and Caffeine uses a frequency sketch.

## Key takeaways

- Move an accessed key exactly one frequency bucket upwards.
- An emptied minimum bucket advances by one because the touched key just entered that next bucket.

## Further reading
- [Constant-time LFU design — Shah, Mitra and Matani](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2110.11602)
- [Python ordered dictionaries](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html)
- [Redis cache eviction policies](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/)

questions.prompt:
Using the lesson's `LFUCache` (ties broken by least recent), capacity 2:

```python
c = LFUCache(2)
# Insert or refresh this cache entry.
c.put(1, 1); c.put(2, 2)
# Read and update cache metadata.
c.get(1)
# Insert or refresh this cache entry.
c.put(3, 3)
# Read and update cache metadata.
c.get(3)
# Insert or refresh this cache entry.
c.put(4, 4)
```

Which key does `put(4, 4)` evict?

options.text: Key 3, because it was inserted most recently
options.explanation: LFU does not evict by insertion time first; it compares counts. And among equal counts it evicts the *least* recently used, not the most.

options.text: Key 4, because a new key has the lowest count
options.explanation: The new key is added after eviction, so it is never a candidate for its own eviction.

options.text: Key 1
options.explanation: Correct. Keys 1 and 3 both have count 2. Key 1 reached count 2 before key 3 did, so it is the oldest in bucket 2 and is evicted.

options.text: Key 2
options.explanation: Key 2 was already evicted by `put(3, 3)`; it is not in the cache when `put(4, 4)` runs.

questions.workedExample:
Track counts and buckets (oldest first):
```
put 1      {1:1}       b1=[1]
put 2      {1:1,2:1}   b1=[1,2]
get 1      {1:2,2:1}   b1=[2] b2=[1]
put 3      full, min_f=1 -> evict 2
           {1:2,3:1}   b1=[3] b2=[1]
get 3      {1:2,3:2}   b2=[1,3]
           b1 empty, min_f -> 2
put 4      full, min_f=2 -> evict
           oldest of b2 = 1
```
Then 4 is inserted with count 1 and `min_f` resets to 1.

questions.prompt: In the LFU `_bump` method, when bucket `f` empties and `min_f == f`, the code sets `min_f = f + 1` without searching. Why is that always correct?

options.text: Because buckets are stored in a sorted structure, so the next one is found in O(1)
options.explanation: The buckets are in a dict ordered by insertion, not by numeric frequency; nothing is searched or sorted.

options.text: Because the key being bumped has just been placed in bucket `f + 1`, so that bucket is non-empty and no smaller one is
options.explanation: Correct. Bucket `f` was the smallest non-empty bucket and is now empty, and the bumped key now has count `f + 1`, so `f + 1` is the new minimum.

options.text: Because counts are capped, so `f + 1` is always the largest bucket
options.explanation: There is no cap on counts in this design, and the question is about the minimum, not the maximum.

options.text: It is not always correct; a full scan is needed occasionally
options.explanation: No scan is ever needed. The only other place `min_f` changes is an insert, which sets it to 1.

questions.workedExample: The old bucket was the lowest occupied one. Moving its last key out empties it, and that key immediately occupies the next count. Nothing can remain below that next count, so it becomes the new minimum. New insertions are the separate case: count one resets the minimum to one. These rules rely on increments of exactly one.

lessons.title: Random choice with constant-time deletion
lessons.summary: Swap the last array item into a deleted slot and repair its map index.
lessons.body:
## Insert, delete and getRandom in O(1)

Design a set supporting `insert(x)`, `remove(x)` and `get_random()` (each element equally likely), all in O(1) average.

- A hash set gives O(1) insert and remove, but no way to pick a uniform random element without walking it.
- An array gives O(1) uniform random choice (`items[randrange(n)]`), but removing from the middle is O(n), where n is the number of elements, because every later element shifts left.

Combine them: an array of values plus a map from value to index. The clever step is deletion. Instead of shifting everything left, **move the last element into the hole** and pop the end, which is O(1).

```
remove(20)
items: [10, 20, 30, 40]   pos[20] = 1
copy last (40) into index 1
items: [10, 40, 30, 40]   pos[40] = 1
pop end, delete pos[20]
items: [10, 40, 30]
```

```python
import random

class RandomizedSet:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []  # the values
        self.pos = {}    # value -> index

    def insert(self, x):
        if x in self.pos:
            return False
        self.pos[x] = len(self.items)
        self.items.append(x)
        return True

    def remove(self, x):
        if x not in self.pos:
            return False
        i = self.pos[x]
        last = self.items[-1]
        self.items[i] = last  # overwrite x
        # Repair the moved value’s lookup
        # index.
        self.pos[last] = i
        self.items.pop()
        # Delete after repair, even if x is
        # last.
        del self.pos[x]
        return True

    def get_random(self):
        return random.choice(self.items)
```

The order of the last two map operations matters. If `x` is itself the last element, `last == x`: we set `pos[x] = i` and then delete `pos[x]`, which is correct. Do it the other way round (delete, then set `pos[last]`) and you resurrect a map entry for a value that is no longer in the array.

`get_random()` requires a non-empty set; Python raises `IndexError` on an empty one.

The array does not preserve insertion order after a removal. That is fine here because a set has no order, but it is the price of O(1) deletion.

With duplicates (a multiset), map each value to a *set of indices*. Removal picks any index of `x`, moves the last element there, and updates the last element's index set. `get_random` still picks one array slot uniformly, so a value that fills more slots comes up more often.

For `items = [1, 1, 2]`, the value 1 has 2 copies out of 3 slots, so it is returned about two times in three and 2 about one time in three. Returning each value with probability proportional to its count is usually what is wanted from a multiset; if you need each *distinct* value equally often, you need a separate array of distinct values to sample from.

## Key takeaways

- Swap the last array item into a deleted slot and repair its map index.
- Sampling array slots weights duplicate values by their number of copies.

## Further reading
- [Python random-number generation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/random.html)
- [Python list and mapping operations](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html)

questions.prompt: In the O(1) `RandomizedSet`, how does `remove(x)` remove an element from the middle of the array without an O(n) shift?

options.text: It marks the slot as deleted and skips such slots in `get_random`
options.explanation: Tombstones keep removal O(1) but break `get_random`: you would have to retry on deleted slots, and the array would grow without bound.

options.text: It sorts the array and binary searches for `x`
options.explanation: Sorting is O(n log n) and binary search is O(log n), where n is the number of elements in the array; neither gives O(1), and the map already knows the index.

options.text: It uses `list.remove(x)`, which is O(1) in Python
options.explanation: `list.remove` scans for the value and shifts every later element left: O(n), where n is the number of elements.

options.text: It copies the last element into `x`'s slot, updates that element's index in the map, and pops the end
options.explanation: Correct. Only the end of the array changes size, and popping the end is amortised O(1), including occasional resizing. The cost is that array order is not preserved, which a set does not need.

questions.workedExample:
Example: `items = [10, 20, 30, 40]`, remove 20.
1. `i = pos[20] = 1`, `last = 40`.
2. `items[1] = 40` gives `[10, 40, 30, 40]`.
3. `pos[40] = 1`.
4. `items.pop()` gives `[10, 40, 30]`.
5. `del pos[20]`.

The operation is expected amortised O(1), accounting for hashing and resizing. Nothing after index 1 moved.

questions.prompt: A `RandomizedSet` holds `items = [10, 20, 30, 40]` with `pos = {10: 0, 20: 1, 30: 2, 40: 3}`. After `remove(10)` then `remove(20)`, what are `items` and `pos`?

options.explanation: This is what deleting and moving later array elements down one slot would produce. The swap-with-last strategy never shifts, so order is not preserved.
The array is right but `pos[40]` is stale. The code updates the moved element's index (`pos[last] = i`) precisely so a later `remove(40)` does not read past the end.
Correct. Removing 10 pulls 40 into index 0; removing 20 pulls 30 into index 1. The map index of each relocated array entry is updated.
This stops after the first removal. The second `remove(20)` also runs and pulls 30 forward.

questions.workedExample:
1. `remove(10)`: `i = 0`, `last = 40`. Copy: `[40, 20, 30, 40]`, set `pos[40] = 0`, pop: `[40, 20, 30]`, delete `pos[10]`.
2. `remove(20)`: `i = 1`, `last = 30`. Copy: `[40, 30, 30]`, set `pos[30] = 1`, pop: `[40, 30]`, delete `pos[20]`.
3. Final: `items = [40, 30]`, `pos = {40: 0, 30: 1}`.

lessons.title: Composite designs and concurrent access
lessons.summary: Match lookup, ordering and sampling needs to complementary structures.
lessons.body:
## Recognising the pattern

| Need | Structure |
|---|---|
| Find by key | Hash map |
| Recency or insertion order | Doubly linked list |
| Uniform random / by index | Dynamic array |
| Min or max, changing | Heap |
| Sorted order, ranges | Balanced BST |

Other classics built the same way:

- **Min stack**: a stack of `(value, min so far)` pairs gives O(1) `get_min`.
- **Time-based key-value store**: map from key to a list of `(timestamp, value)` appended in time order, then binary search, for O(log n) "value at time t", where n is the number of timestamps stored for that key and t is the time asked about.
- **All O(1) data structure** (increment, decrement, get max key, get min key): the LFU bucket idea, with a doubly linked list of count buckets.

## Pitfalls

- Forgetting one side. A common bug is the two structures drifting apart: a key left in the map after its node was evicted, or an index pointing at a moved element.
- Average, not worst case. The O(1) relies on hash map operations being O(1) on average. Adversarial keys can degrade them.
- **Capacity edge cases.** Capacity 0, updating an existing key when full (no eviction should happen), and removing the last element are where interview solutions break.
- **Concurrency.** A cache-hit `get` on this LRU implementation writes recency pointers. Concurrent access needs a correct synchronisation strategy, commonly a lock around operations; a miss does not move a node. This is one reason high-throughput caches approximate LRU instead.

## Key takeaways

- Match lookup, ordering and sampling needs to complementary structures.
- Capacity limits and concurrent recency writes must preserve every structure together.

## Further reading
- [CPython’s LRU cache implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.14.0/Lib/functools.py)
- [Python ordered dictionaries](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html)
- [Redis cache eviction policies](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/)

questions.prompt: You are putting an in-process LRU cache in front of a service handling many concurrent requests. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A cache-hit `get` mutates recency pointers and needs write synchronisation
options.explanation: Correct. A hit moves the node to the front, which is a write to shared pointers. Two unsynchronised `get`s can corrupt the list.

options.text: A read-write lock lets `get` calls run in parallel safely, because they only read
options.explanation: This is the trap: in LRU, `get` is not read-only. Holding only a read lock while relinking nodes is a data race.

options.text: The O(1) bounds are average-case, because they rest on hash map operations
options.explanation: Correct. With many colliding keys a hash map degrades, so the structure is O(1) on average, not in the worst case.

options.text: Swapping LRU for a heap-based LFU would keep every operation O(1)
options.explanation: A heap update costs O(log n), where n is the number of keys in the cache. O(1) LFU needs the frequency-bucket design.

options.text: `OrderedDict` and Java's `LinkedHashMap` implement the same hash-map-plus-linked-list idea
options.explanation: Correct. Both pair a hash table with a doubly linked list of entries, which is why they can do LRU in a few lines.

questions.workedExample:
1. Look at `get`: it calls `_unlink` and `_push_front`, six pointer assignments in this implementation. So a hit is a write.
2. Hence a read-write lock gives no parallelism for hits; a mutex around this implementation is one solution; sharding and approximate eviction policies offer other designs.
3. All the O(1) claims inherit the hash map's average-case guarantee.
4. A heap keyed on count needs a possible sift when an access changes its count: O(log n), where n is the number of keys in the cache (at most 19 swaps for a million keys).
5. `OrderedDict.move_to_end` and `LinkedHashMap(accessOrder=true)` are the library versions of the lesson's code.

lessons.title: Representing disjoint sets with parent forests
lessons.summary: A root represents its entire connected component.
lessons.body:
**Union-Find** (also called a **disjoint-set union**, or DSU) keeps track of elements split into non-overlapping groups. It supports two operations:

- `find(x)`: which group is `x` in? It returns a **set representative** element for the group.
- `union(a, b)`: merge the groups containing `a` and `b`.

Two elements are in the same group exactly when `find(a) == find(b)`. That one comparison answers "are these connected?" for road networks, friend circles, pixels in an image or accounts that share an email address.

With balancing and path compression, long sequences of operations have a very small amortised cost. This does not make every individual operation constant-time.

## The idea: a forest of parent pointers

Each group is a tree. Every element points to a parent; the root points to itself and is the group's representative. All you store is one array, `parent`.

```
parent = [0, 0, 1, 3, 3]

  0       3
  |       |
  1       4
  |
  2
groups: {0, 1, 2} and {3, 4}
```

- `find(x)` follows parent pointers up to the root.
- `union(a, b)` finds both roots and makes one the parent of the other.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Group representatives
> Two clubs merge by choosing one representative for the combined club.
>
> **How it maps:** Following a member's chain of representatives reaches the current root. Members belong to the same group when those chains reach the same representative.
>
> **Where it stops:** Parent pointers are bookkeeping, not the original friendships or network links. Changing the representative does not reveal paths or distances between members.

The naive version has a problem. Union in an unlucky order (`union(1, 0)`, `union(2, 1)`, `union(3, 2)` and so on, always hanging the old tree under the new element) builds a chain, and `find` on the bottom element walks every link in it: one fewer link than there are elements. If n is the number of elements, a sequence of operations can cost O(n) each in the worst case (O(n) means "grows in proportion to n").

## Key takeaways

- A root represents its entire connected component.
- Compare roots rather than immediate parents.

## Further reading
- [Disjoint-set unions — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/disjoint_set_union.html)

questions.prompt: A union-find structure has `parent = [0, 0, 1, 3, 3]`. Which statement is true?

options.text: 2 and 0 are in different sets, because `parent[2] = 1` and `parent[0] = 0`
options.explanation: This compares parents, not roots. Following 2 → 1 → 0 reaches root 0, the same root as 0 itself.

options.text: 2 and 0 are in the same set, because both lead to root 0
options.explanation: Correct. `find(2)` follows 2 → 1 → 0. `find(0)` is 0. Same root means same set: `{0, 1, 2}`. The other set is `{3, 4}` with root 3.

options.text: 4 and 1 are in the same set, because both have a parent other than themselves
options.explanation: Having a parent just means a node is not a root. 4 leads to root 3 and 1 leads to root 0, so they are in different sets.

options.text: There are five sets, one per element
options.explanation: Only roots (where `parent[x] == x`) start sets: 0 and 3. So there are two sets.

2. Follow each element to its root:
```

1 -> 0
2 -> 1 -> 0
3 -> 3
4 -> 3
```
3. Sets: `{0, 1, 2}` and `{3, 4}`.
4. Connectivity is always `find(a) == find(b)`, never `parent[a] == parent[b]`.

lessons.title: Balancing Union-Find by size and rank
lessons.summary: Attach smaller trees under larger ones to limit depth.
lessons.body:
## Fix 1: union by size or by rank

When merging, **hang the smaller tree under the larger one**. "Smaller" can mean:

- size: number of elements in the tree, or
- **rank**: an upper bound on the tree's height. Every element starts with rank 0.

For rank, attach the lower-rank root under the higher-rank root. If the ranks are equal, choose either root and increase its rank by one. Two rank-two roots therefore produce rank three; adding a singleton to a rank-three root leaves its rank unchanged.

For union by size, an element only gets deeper when its tree joins one at least as big. Its containing tree therefore at least doubles each time it gets deeper. It cannot double indefinitely inside a fixed population: this bounds the depth logarithmically in the number of elements n.

Union by rank has a similar guarantee. A rank increase requires two roots of the same rank, so high ranks require many elements. Parent ranks strictly increase along a path. Rank is an upper bound on height, even after path compression shortens paths without changing ranks.

Both strategies give O(log n) worst-case `find` before compression. The guarantee relies on always joining roots using the chosen rule; linking arbitrary nodes can detach part of a component.

Size is often more useful in practice, because you get the group sizes for free ("how big is the largest friend circle?").

## Key takeaways

- Attach smaller trees under larger ones to limit depth.
- Rank grows only when equal-rank roots merge and remains an upper bound after compression.

## Further reading
- [Disjoint-set unions — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/disjoint_set_union.html)

questions.prompt: With union by size, an element gets one level deeper only when its component joins one at least as large. Why does this prevent a long linear chain?

options.text: Every union rewrites every parent pointer to the root.
options.explanation: That describes compression work; union by size only links roots.

options.text: Each component is required to contain an odd number of elements.
options.explanation: No parity restriction exists.

options.text: Every increase in depth at least doubles the element’s containing component.
options.explanation: Correct. A fixed population permits only logarithmically many such doublings.

options.text: A component’s representative can never change.
options.explanation: A smaller component’s representative becomes a child when components merge.

questions.workedExample: Follow one element. Its depth rises only when its whole tree is attached beneath a tree at least as large. Its new component is at least twice as large, so repeated depth increases require rapidly growing components. This yields logarithmic depth without needing path compression.

questions.prompt: A DSU uses **union by rank** (ties: the first root stays root and its rank rises by one). Starting with five singletons of rank 0, you run `union(0,1)`, `union(2,3)`, `union(0,2)`, `union(4,0)`. What is the final root, and its rank?

options.text: Root 4, rank 1
options.explanation: 4 is a rank-0 singleton and 0's root has rank 2; the lower rank goes underneath, so 4 cannot become the root.

options.text: Root 0, rank 3
options.explanation: Rank only increases when two *equal* ranks merge. The last union is rank 0 into rank 2, which leaves the rank at 2.

options.text: Root 2, rank 2
options.explanation: In `union(0, 2)` the ranks tie, so the first argument's root (0) stays root.

options.text: Root 0, rank 2
options.explanation: Correct. Two rank-0 merges give rank-1 roots 0 and 2; merging those ties, so 0 becomes rank 2; then 4 (rank 0) goes under 0 with no change.

questions.workedExample:
```
u(0,1)  rank 0 = 0  -> 1 under 0, r[0]=1
u(2,3)  rank 0 = 0  -> 3 under 2, r[2]=1
u(0,2)  rank 1 = 1  -> 2 under 0, r[0]=2
u(4,0)  rank 0 < 2  -> 4 under 0, r[0]=2
```
The tree's actual height is 2 (3 → 2 → 0), matching the rank. After later finds compress paths, the height may drop, but the rank stays 2: it is only an upper bound.

lessons.title: Path compression and the DSU implementation
lessons.summary: Find the root, then repoint the visited path at it.
lessons.body:
## Fix 2: path compression

`find` already walks from `x` to the root. While doing so, **repoint every node on the path directly at the root**. Without an intervening union, the next `find` on a non-root node on that path takes one parent step.

```
before find(4)        after find(4)
     0                     0
     |                  / | | \
     1                 1  2 3  4
     |
     2
     |
     3
     |
     4
```

Variants such as **path halving** (point each node at its grandparent as you go) achieve the same bounds in a single pass.

## The full structure

```python
class DSU:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))
        self.size = [1] * n
        self.count = n   # number of sets

    def find(self, x):
        root = x
        while self.parent[root] != root:
            # Follow ancestors to the
            # representative.
            root = self.parent[root]
        # second pass: compress the path
        while self.parent[x] != root:
            # Save the old link before
            # overwriting it.
            nxt = self.parent[x]
            self.parent[x] = root
            x = nxt
        return root

    def union(self, a, b):
        ra, rb = self.find(a), self.find(b)
        if ra == rb:
            return False   # already joined
        if self.size[ra] < self.size[rb]:
            ra, rb = rb, ra
        # smaller tree goes under bigger
        # Join roots; never detach a non-
        # root.
        self.parent[rb] = ra
        self.size[ra] += self.size[rb]
        self.count -= 1
        return True
```

> [!tip] Iterative find in Python
> The textbook recursive `find` (`parent[x] = find(parent[x])`) is elegant, but an unbalanced variant can create a chain exceeding the interpreter's recursion limit. Union by size or rank already prevents such linear-depth chains. The two-pass loop above has no such limit.

Note that `union` returns whether a merge actually happened. That boolean is what most applications use.

## Key takeaways

- Find the root, then repoint the visited path at it.
- Union returns false when its two arguments already share a root.

## Further reading
- [Disjoint-set unions — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/disjoint_set_union.html)

This misses `union(1, 3)`: it finds roots 0 and 2 and links them, so there are only two sets.
Correct. `union(1, 3)` finds roots 0 and 2 (sizes 2 and 2, a tie) and sets `parent[2] = 0`. Node 3 keeps pointing at 2.

options.explanation: Removing compression makes finds slower but keeps the deep chain, so the recursion depth problem stays.

options.text: The parent list is too large for memory
options.explanation: The reported exception identifies excessive recursion; `RecursionError` is about stack depth, not heap memory.

options.explanation: This can crash the interpreter with a real C stack overflow, and leaves the O(n) first find in place. Fix the structure instead.

Recursive find must traverse that chain before its return path can compress it, so compression cannot prevent the first deep recursion. Union by size limits height, and the iterative two-pass find removes the recursive-call requirement. Raising a recursion limit does not repair the long path and can cause resource exhaustion.

lessons.title: Understanding inverse-Ackermann bounds
lessons.summary: Initialisation and later operations have separate costs.
lessons.body:
## How fast is it?

In this table n is the number of elements and m counts the complete sequence of finds and unions, including the unions that create any long path. Initialisation is charged separately. O(f) means "grows at most in proportion to f".

| Version | Cost per operation |
|---|---|
| Naive | O(n) worst case |
| Union by size or rank | O(log n) worst case |
| Path compression only | O(log n) amortised |
| Both | O(α(n)) amortised |

**α(n)** is the inverse Ackermann function. It grows so slowly that it is a tiny number for any practical input size. Its exact small value depends on the convention used to define it. You do not need an Ackermann table to choose or implement Union-Find.

The practical distinction is between a bound for one operation and a bound for a complete sequence. Balancing limits how long one root path can be; compression makes later traversals cheaper by repairing paths already visited.

“Amortised” matters: one `find` may still traverse a logarithmic path, then flatten it. Across m finds and unions on n initially separate elements, later work is O(m α(n)), plus O(n) to initialise the arrays. These bounds describe growth, not measured pointer counts. They include the operations that built the paths; do not start the analysis from an arbitrary uncharged tree.

> [!note] Rank after compression
> Path compression changes heights but never updates ranks. That is fine: rank was only ever an *upper bound* on height, but the inverse-Ackermann proof also uses rank-growth and node-count invariants, not just this upper bound.

## Key takeaways

- Initialisation and later operations have separate costs.
- Inverse-Ackermann bounds apply to a sequence, not a fixed operation-step count.

## Further reading
- [Disjoint-set unions — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/disjoint_set_union.html)

questions.prompt: Which statements about union-find complexity are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: With balancing and compression, the inverse-Ackermann bound describes amortised work over a sequence.
options.explanation: Correct. Its very slow growth makes the amortised cost tiny for practical inputs, but it is not a constant worst-case promise for each find.

options.text: With both optimisations, every single `find` takes O(1) worst-case time
options.explanation: The bound is amortised. One `find` can still walk an O(log n) path the first time, though it flattens that path for next time.

options.text: Path compression alone (no union by rank) gives O(log n) amortised per operation
options.explanation: Correct. Compression on its own is already logarithmic amortised; adding rank brings it down to α(n).

options.text: Path compression updates ranks so that rank always equals exact height
options.explanation: Ranks are never updated by compression; they become upper bounds on height, while the proof also uses how ranks grow and bound node counts.

options.text: Union by size alone guarantees O(log n) worst-case `find`
options.explanation: Correct. The doubling argument gives a logarithmic height bound in the number of elements, so each find is O(log n) even in the worst case.

questions.workedExample: Here n counts elements. Balancing alone limits each root path logarithmically. Compression alone gives a logarithmic amortised bound when the sequence includes the operations creating its paths. Combining them gives an inverse-Ackermann amortised bound. A particular find may still traverse a logarithmic path. Compression shortens actual height without recalculating ranks; rank remains an upper bound with the required growth invariants.

lessons.title: Kruskal and incremental connectivity
lessons.summary: Kruskal accepts exactly the edges that join different components.
lessons.body:
## Application 1: Kruskal's minimum spanning tree

Kruskal's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree by taking edges cheapest first and keeping an edge only if it joins two different components. "Different components?" is exactly `find(u) != find(v)`, and keeping the edge is `union(u, v)`.

```python
def kruskal(n, edges):
    # edges: list of (weight, u, v)
    dsu = DSU(n)
    total, used = 0, []
    for w, u, v in sorted(edges):
        # Keep edges only between
        # components.
        if dsu.union(u, v):
            total += w
            used.append((u, v))
    return total, used
```

For V vertices and E unsorted edges, initialising the DSU takes O(V), comparison-sorting the edges takes O(E log E), and processing them takes O(E α(V)) with balancing and compression. Sorting dominates for a connected graph; if a disconnected graph has many isolated vertices, initialisation can matter instead.

On disconnected input the code returns a minimum spanning forest. In a connected graph you can stop once the chosen edges connect every vertex: the tree then has one fewer edge than vertices.

## Application 2: connectivity and cycle detection

- Number of connected components: start with `count = n` and decrement on every successful union. Edges can arrive one at a time ("number of islands II", or a network where links come up over time), and you can answer after each one.
- **Cycle detection in an undirected graph**: adding edge (u, v) when `find(u) == find(v)` closes a cycle. `union` returning `False` is the signal. This is the "redundant connection" problem.
- **Percolation**: a grid percolates when a virtual top node and a virtual bottom node end up in the same set, a classic Monte Carlo experiment.

Compared with BFS or DFS, union-find shines when edges arrive incrementally. A straightforward BFS test of graph reachability may traverse the current graph for each request; union-find just absorbs each new edge.

## Key takeaways

- Kruskal accepts exactly the edges that join different components.
- A failed union detects a cycle in an undirected incremental graph.

## Further reading
- [Disjoint-set unions — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/disjoint_set_union.html)

options.explanation: Correct. The E union-find operations cost O(E α(V)), where α is the extremely slowly growing inverse Ackermann function. For this connected graph, comparison sorting is the asymptotic bottleneck.

options.text: The union-find operations, O(E log V) each
options.explanation: With both optimisations each operation is O(α(V)) amortised, not O(log V), and certainly not that much per operation.

(2,3)  {1,2,3}          True

lessons.title: Accounts merging and Union-Find variants
lessons.summary: Shared identifiers create a transitive closure of account groups.
lessons.body:
## Application 3: accounts merge

Each account is a name plus a list of emails. In this exercise, sharing an email is a trusted signal to merge accounts, and we take its transitive closure: A shares with B and B shares with C, so all three join one component. Directly sharing an email is not itself transitive. Assume each account has at least one email and merged accounts have consistent names; real entity resolution needs stronger domain rules.

Union the account indices through shared emails:

```python
def merge_accounts(accounts):
    dsu = DSU(len(accounts))
    owner = {}   # email -> account index
    for i, acc in enumerate(accounts):
        for email in acc[1:]:
            if email in owner:
                # Shared email joins account
                # components.
                dsu.union(i, owner[email])
            else:
                owner[email] = i
    groups = {}
    for email, i in owner.items():
        # Group each unique email under its
        # root.
        r = dsu.find(i)
        groups.setdefault(r, [])
        groups[r].append(email)
    return [[accounts[r][0]] + sorted(es)
            for r, es in groups.items()]
```

The same shape appears in **entity resolution** (deduplicating customer records that share a phone number or address), clustering, and compilers: type inference in ML-family languages unifies type variables with a union-find structure.

## Variants worth knowing

- **Weighted union-find** stores, for each node, a value relative to its parent (an offset, a ratio, a bit recording whether a path length is odd or even). `find` accumulates values along the path. This solves "evaluate division" (given some ratios between variables, work out others) and "is this graph bipartite?" online.

For example, if one quantity is twice a second and the second is three times a third, the first is six times the third. A weighted parent link stores one such relation; following the path combines them. Compression must update those relations along with the parent pointers.

- **Offline deletion**: union-find cannot split a set. For a known deletion-only history, first build the final graph, then process removals backwards as additions. Mixed additions and deletions need extra machinery.
- Hash-map parents: when elements are strings or sparse coordinates, use a dict instead of a list, creating entries on first sight.

## Pitfalls

- Comparing parents, not roots. `parent[a] == parent[b]` is not the same as being connected. Always compare `find(a)` and `find(b)`.
- Linking non-roots. `parent[b] = a` instead of `parent[find(b)] = find(a)` loses the rest of b's tree.
- Forgetting it is undirected. Union-find has no notion of direction, so it cannot detect cycles in a directed graph or find strongly connected components. Use DFS-based algorithms for those.

## Key takeaways

- Shared identifiers create a transitive closure of account groups.
- Weighted parents carry relations; known deletion-only histories can be processed backwards.

## Further reading

lessons.title: Answering ranges from stored tree pieces
lessons.summary: Each node summarises one contiguous range.
lessons.body:
Here n is the non-empty input array’s length. Big-O bounds count constant-time combines of constant-size summaries on word-sized values.

Suppose you have an array and two kinds of request arriving in any order: "what is the sum (or minimum, or maximum) of `a[l..r]`?" and "change `a[i]`".

Throughout this lesson n is the number of elements in the array, and O(f) means "the work grows at most in proportion to f". `a[l..r]` means the elements from index l to index r, both included.

- A plain array makes updates O(1) (a fixed amount of work) but queries O(n).
- A prefix-sum array makes sum queries O(1) but every update O(n), because every later prefix changes.

On large arrays, many linear-time operations become expensive. A **segment tree** balances the trade-off: point updates and range queries each take O(log n), provided each summary has constant size and combining two summaries takes constant time. It works for associative operations, including sums, minima and maxima.

## The idea: store answers for halves, quarters, eighths...

Each node of a segment tree is responsible for a contiguous range of the array and stores the answer for that range. The root covers everything; each node splits its range in half between its two children; the leaves are single elements.

For `a = [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7, 4]` with sums:

```
              [0,7]=39
         /              \
    [0,3]=16          [4,7]=23
    /      \          /      \
 [0,1]=7 [2,3]=9  [4,5]=12 [6,7]=11
  / \     / \      / \      / \
 5   2   8   1    9   3    7   4
```

A query for indices 2 through 5 uses the stored nodes for 2 through 3 and 4 through 5. Their totals, 9 and 12, give 21. The query stops at those nodes because each is fully covered; it need not visit their leaves.

Only the two ends of a requested range can cut through nodes at each level. Everything between them uses fully covered pieces, which is why a query needs only logarithmically many nodes.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Totals by district
> A delivery service keeps parcel totals for regions, districts and streets.
>
> **How it maps:** A request covering a whole district uses its stored total; only partly covered districts need smaller pieces. Segment-tree nodes similarly summarise nested contiguous ranges.
>
> **Where it stops:** The tree uses fixed binary splits, and its combine must be associative. Geographic districts need not satisfy either rule.

## Key takeaways

- Each node summarises one contiguous range.
- Fully covered pieces combine into the requested range without scanning all elements.

## Further reading
- [Segment trees — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/segment_tree.html)

lessons.summary: Use one-based child indices in a flat array.

## Storing it in an array

Like a binary heap, the recursive tree lives in a flat array with its root at index one. In code, the children of node `v` are `2 * v` and `2 * v + 1`; no child pointers are stored.

When the element count is a power of two, the tree fills its levels neatly. Other lengths leave gaps in this numbering. Allocating `4 * n` slots is a safe bound for a non-empty input of n elements; it does not mean the tree contains four nodes per element.

To see why the bound is safe, round the leaf capacity up to a power of two. That increases the capacity by less than a factor of two; a full binary tree needs fewer than twice that many nodes. The spare slot at index zero also fits. With eight elements, sixteen slots suffice. With six elements, recursive midpoint splitting reaches index thirteen, so twelve slots would be too few.

## Key takeaways

- Use one-based child indices in a flat array.
- Round the leaf capacity up to a power of two when bounding allocated slots.

## Further reading
- [Segment trees — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/segment_tree.html)

For six elements, midpoint splitting reaches index thirteen, so twelve slots are too few. This is an allocation bound, not a claim of four nodes per element.

lessons.title: Building, querying and updating segment trees
lessons.summary: Disjoint, covered and partial overlap are the three query cases.
lessons.body:
Here n is the non-empty input array’s length. Big-O bounds count constant-time combines of constant-size summaries on word-sized values.

## Query, update and build

The examples require a non-empty array. Both endpoints of a query and the position of an update must lie inside it; a query's end must not precede its start. The methods assume callers enforce that contract.

For eight elements, `query(2, 5)` is valid, while `query(5, 2)` and `update(8, x)` are invalid. Integer sums are associative; floating-point sums need numerical-error considerations.

```python
class SegTree:
    def __init__(self, a):
        self.n = len(a)
        if not self.n:
            raise ValueError("empty array")
        self.t = [0] * (4 * self.n)
        self._build(a, 1, 0, self.n - 1)

    def _pull(self, v):
        t = self.t
        # Restore this parent from child
        # sums.
        t[v] = t[2*v] + t[2*v + 1]

    def _build(self, a, v, lo, hi):
        # A leaf represents one array
        # element.
        if lo == hi:
            self.t[v] = a[lo]
            return
        m = (lo + hi) // 2
        self._build(a, 2*v, lo, m)
        self._build(a, 2*v + 1, m + 1, hi)
        # Recompute after either child
        # changes.
        self._pull(v)

    def query(self, l, r):  # inclusive
        return self._q(1, 0, self.n-1, l, r)

    def _q(self, v, lo, hi, l, r):
        if r < lo or hi < l:     # disjoint
            return 0
        if l <= lo and hi <= r:  # covered
            # A covered node already has the
            # answer.
            return self.t[v]
        m = (lo + hi) // 2
        return (self._q(2*v, lo, m, l, r) +
            self._q(2*v+1, m+1, hi, l, r))

    def update(self, i, x):
        self._u(1, 0, self.n-1, i, x)

    def _u(self, v, lo, hi, i, x):
        # A leaf represents one array
        # element.
        if lo == hi:
            self.t[v] = x
            return
        m = (lo + hi) // 2
        if i <= m:
            self._u(2*v, lo, m, i, x)
        else:
            self._u(2*v+1, m+1, hi, i, x)
        # Recompute after either child
        # changes.
        self._pull(v)
```

The query has three cases at each node:

1. **Disjoint**: the node's range misses `[l, r]` entirely. Return the identity (0 for sum, +infinity for min).
2. Covered: the node's range lies inside `[l, r]`. Return its stored value without going deeper.
3. Partial overlap: recurse into both children and combine.

The update walks one root-to-leaf path, then recomputes each node on the way back up.

### Why O(log n)?

- Build: every node (twice the element count, minus one) is computed once: O(n).
- **Update**: one root-to-leaf path, O(1) work per node: O(log n).
- **Query**: at each level, at most two nodes are *partially* overlapped (the ones containing the ends of `[l, r]`). Everything between them is fully covered and stops immediately. So at most four nodes are visited per level.

Both operations therefore take O(log n) work, whereas building touches every node once and takes O(n). The complexity assumes constant-time combines; storing larger summaries changes that cost.

## Key takeaways

- Disjoint, covered and partial overlap are the three query cases.
- Point updates recompute summaries on one root-to-leaf path.

## Further reading
- [Segment trees — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/segment_tree.html)

lessons.title: Combining summaries and maximum subarrays
lessons.summary: An associative combine and an empty-range identity define a valid range summary.
lessons.body:
Here n is the non-empty input array’s length. Big-O bounds count constant-time combines of constant-size summaries on word-sized values.

## Beyond sums: what can a node store?

The structure works whenever the combine operation is **associative**, with an **identity element** for the empty range:

Associativity means adjacent pieces can be grouped differently without changing the result. An identity is a neutral summary that leaves another summary unchanged: zero for sums, positive infinity for minima, and negative infinity for maxima.

Sum, min, max, gcd (greatest common divisor), bitwise AND, bitwise OR, bitwise XOR and matrix products all qualify. Subtraction does not: subtracting three and then two from eight gives three, while subtracting their difference from eight gives seven.

Associative is enough; commutative is not required. The recursive code always combines the left child before the right, so non-commutative operations like matrix multiplication or string concatenation work, as long as you keep that order. Actual string concatenation is not constant-time, and matrix costs depend on dimension; their runtimes include combine costs.

You can also store a small **struct** per node. The famous example is the **maximum subarray sum** over a range, with point updates. Each node stores four numbers:

| Field | Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `sum` | s | total of the range |
| `pre` | p | best prefix sum |
| `suf` | q | best suffix sum |
| `best` | b | best subarray sum |

To combine children, add their totals. A prefix either stays in the left child or includes the whole left child plus a right prefix; a suffix works symmetrically. The best subarray either stays in one child or crosses the split, joining a left suffix to a right prefix. The exact update rules are useful implementation reference:

```formula reference
s = s_L + s_R
p = max(p_L, s_L + p_R)
q = max(q_R, s_R + q_L)
b = max(b_L, b_R, q_L + p_R)
where
s, p, q, b: the combined total, best prefix sum, best suffix sum and best non-empty subarray sum
s_L, p_L, q_L, b_L: those four summaries for the left child
s_R, p_R, q_R, b_R: those four summaries for the right child
max: the largest argument
In words: a prefix either stays in the left half or includes that whole half; a suffix is symmetric. The best subarray stays in one half or joins a left suffix to a right prefix.
```

For example, take the left half [2, −1] and the right half [3, −5]:

The best subarray of `[2, -1, 3, -5]` is `[2, -1, 3]`, with total 4. It crosses the split: the best suffix of the left half joins the best prefix of the right half.

These rules assume non-empty subarrays. For an empty-range identity use a total of zero and negative infinity for the other three fields; a real leaf uses its value for all four fields.

The best subarray is either entirely in one half or crosses the middle, in which case it is a suffix of the left plus a prefix of the right. Kadane's algorithm cannot handle updates; this can, in O(log n) each.

## Key takeaways

- An associative combine and an empty-range identity define a valid range summary.
- Maximum-subarray nodes retain total, best prefix, best suffix and best interior sum.

lessons.title: Lazy range updates and deferred tags
lessons.summary: A fully covered node updates its summary immediately.
lessons.body:
Here n is the non-empty input array’s length. Big-O bounds count constant-time combines of constant-size summaries on word-sized values.

## Lazy propagation: updating whole ranges

Now add a third request: “add the same amount to every element in this range”. Running a separate point update for each element repeats many root-to-leaf traversals and can take O(n log n) for a whole-array update.

**Lazy propagation** stops at fully covered nodes. It updates the node's summary immediately, then leaves a **pending tag** recording work still owed to its children. For a sum, add the increment once per covered element; for the tag, accumulate the increment once.

For example, adding five to four zeros makes the covering node's sum twenty and its pending addition five. Its children remain untouched. A later operation must push that addition before descending into them, so stale child summaries never answer a query directly.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A team-wide instruction
> A manager records a change for an entire team, passing it to subteams only when their individual records are needed.
>
> **How it maps:** The parent already records the team's new total; the pending instruction represents updates still owed to children. Descending requires passing the instruction on first.
>
> **Where it stops:** This works only when the summary can be updated without inspecting each member and instructions can be combined correctly. Arbitrary data changes do not have those properties.

## Key takeaways

- A fully covered node updates its summary immediately.
- A pending tag records work still owed to the children.

## Further reading
- [Segment trees — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/segment_tree.html)

lessons.title: Pushing and composing lazy updates
lessons.summary: Push pending updates before descending into children, including during queries.
lessons.body:
Here n is the non-empty input array’s length. Big-O bounds count constant-time combines of constant-size summaries on word-sized values.

## Implementing deferred updates

The following complete sum-tree example starts from zeros and uses valid inclusive ranges. Its pending tag has the meaning introduced in the previous unit.

```python
class LazySeg:
    def __init__(self, n):
        if n < 1:
            raise ValueError("n > 0")
        self.n = n
        self.t = [0] * (4 * n)   # sums
        self.lz = [0] * (4 * n)  # pending

    def _apply(self, v, lo, hi, x):
        # add x to every element under v
        self.t[v] += x * (hi - lo + 1)
        self.lz[v] += x

    def _push(self, v, lo, hi):
        x = self.lz[v]
        if x:
            m = (lo + hi) // 2
            self._apply(2*v, lo, m, x)
            self._apply(2*v+1, m+1, hi, x)
            # Children now own the deferred
            # addition.
            self.lz[v] = 0

    def add(self, l, r, x):
        self._add(1, 0, self.n-1, l, r, x)

    def _add(self, v, lo, hi, l, r, x):
        if r < lo or hi < l:
            return
        if l <= lo and hi <= r:
            self._apply(v, lo, hi, x)
            return
        # Make child summaries current
        # first.
        self._push(v, lo, hi)
        m = (lo + hi) // 2
        self._add(2*v, lo, m, l, r, x)
        self._add(2*v+1, m+1, hi, l, r, x)
        t = self.t
        # Restore this parent from child
        # sums.
        t[v] = t[2*v] + t[2*v + 1]

    def query(self, l, r):
        return self._q(1, 0, self.n-1, l, r)

    def _q(self, v, lo, hi, l, r):
        if r < lo or hi < l:
            return 0
        if l <= lo and hi <= r:
            # A covered node already has the
            # answer.
            return self.t[v]
        # Make child summaries current
        # first.
        self._push(v, lo, hi)
        m = (lo + hi) // 2
        return (self._q(2*v, lo, m, l, r) +
            self._q(2*v+1, m+1, hi, l, r))
```

> [!example] Tracing a lazy update
> On 8 zeros, `add(0, 3, 5)` reaches node `[0,3]`, which is fully covered. It sets that node's sum to 20 and its tag to 5, and the root's sum to 20. The four leaves are not touched at all. A later `add(2, 5, 1)` must go inside `[0,3]`, so it first pushes the tag: `[0,1]` and `[2,3]` each get sum 10 and tag 5.

Both operations now visit O(log n) nodes, so range update and range query are both **O(log n)**.

Lazy propagation needs two properties:

- You can update a node's summary without looking at its children.
- Pending tags **compose**: two adds become one add. Mixing "assign" and "add" works too, but the tag must record the order (an assignment wipes out earlier adds).

For a range add, the sum rises by the increment once per element; the minimum rises by the increment once. Two pending additions combine by adding their increments. A later assignment replaces earlier additions, while an addition after an assignment still changes the assigned value.

For example, adding three, assigning seven and then adding two has the same effect as assigning nine, regardless of the original values.

Some updates fail the first test. "Replace each range element with its remainder after division by a positive integer" changes a sum in a way that depends on every element, so plain lazy propagation cannot do it.

## Key takeaways

- Push pending updates before descending into children, including during queries.
- Tag composition must preserve update order when assignments and additions mix.

lessons.title: Iterative segment trees and practical choices
lessons.summary: A bottom-up tree puts leaves in the second half of its array.
lessons.body:
Here n is the non-empty input array’s length. Big-O bounds count constant-time combines of constant-size summaries on word-sized values.

## The iterative bottom-up version

For point updates and commutative operations there is a compact non-recursive form. For n input elements it uses `2 * n` slots: element `a[j]` lives at `t[n + j]`. The parent of an index `i` is `i // 2`. The code below builds the tree and answers half-open ranges, including an empty range.

```python
def build(a):
    n = len(a)
    t = [0] * n + list(a)
    for i in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
        t[i] = t[2*i] + t[2*i + 1]
    return t

def query(t, n, l, r):  # half-open [l, r)
    res = 0
    l, r = l + n, r + n
    while l < r:
        if l & 1:   # l is a right child
            # Include the exposed left-edge
            # block.
            res += t[l]
            l += 1
        if r & 1:   # r - 1 is a left child
            r -= 1
            # Include the exposed right-edge
            # block.
            res += t[r]
        l, r = l // 2, r // 2
    return res
```

It avoids recursive-call overhead.

Benchmark recursive and iterative implementations on the intended workload before claiming a speedup.

## Where segment trees are used

- Competitive programming and interviews: range sum/min/max with updates, "count of smaller numbers after self" (after coordinate compression), and booking problems such as "maximum number of overlapping events" (range add plus range max).
- **Computational geometry**: sweep-line algorithms, such as computing the area of a union of rectangles, keep a segment tree over the y-coordinates.
- **Huge index ranges**: a dynamic (sparse) segment tree creates nodes only when touched, so it can cover indices up to a billion with memory proportional to the operations performed.

> [!note] A name clash
> In computational geometry, "segment tree" traditionally names a related structure that stores a set of *intervals* and answers "which intervals contain point x?" in O(log n + k), where n is the number of stored intervals and k is the number of intervals reported. The array-based segment tree in this lesson is the meaning used in competitive programming and interviews.

## Pitfalls

- Inclusive vs half-open ranges. Pick one convention and stick to it; mixing them is the most common bug.
- **Wrong identity.** Returning 0 for a disjoint range in a *min* tree silently corrupts answers. Use +infinity.
- Forgetting to push. In a lazy tree, every operation that descends past a node must push its tag first, including queries.
- Overkill. If you only need prefix sums with point updates, a Fenwick tree (next lesson) is shorter and often has lower overhead; measure the actual workload. If the array never changes, a prefix-sum array or sparse table is simpler still.

## Key takeaways

- A bottom-up tree puts leaves in the second half of its array.
- Keep half-open ranges distinct from inclusive ranges and choose the simplest structure for the workload.

lessons.title: Prefix sums as binary-sized blocks
lessons.summary: Subtract two prefix totals to answer a range sum.
lessons.body:
Here n is the number of input elements. Fenwick positions start at 1; the empty prefix is valid, but an update at zero is not. Arithmetic costs assume word-sized values.

A **Fenwick tree**, or **binary indexed tree** (BIT), maintains point updates and prefix sums: totals from position one through a chosen endpoint. To obtain a range sum, subtract the prefix before its left end from the prefix through its right end. The empty prefix totals zero.

For example, if the prefix through position two totals seven and the prefix through position five totals twenty-five, positions three through five total eighteen. This cancellation works because subtraction undoes addition. Two prefix minima cannot be cancelled this way.

What it gives up in generality it repays in simplicity. The whole structure is one array of n + 1 numbers and two loops of about four lines each. Historical accounts commonly credit Boris Ryabko’s 1989 coding work. Peter Fenwick’s 1994 paper presents the binary indexed tree for cumulative-frequency tables in arithmetic-coding compression.

## The intuition: binary decomposition of a prefix

Any positive whole number is a sum of distinct powers of two. Thirteen uses eight, four and one, so its prefix can be tiled by positions 1–8, 9–12 and 13.

A Fenwick entry stores the block ending at its own index. Its block length is the value of that index's **lowest set bit**, the rightmost one in binary. A prefix query reads its final block, then the preceding block, until the entire prefix is covered without overlap.

Each step removes one set bit. An index has only logarithmically many bits, so the query needs O(log n) stored blocks rather than a scan of n elements.

## Key takeaways

- Subtract two prefix totals to answer a range sum.
- A prefix decomposes into one block for each set bit in its index.

## Further reading
- [Fenwick trees — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/fenwick.html)

lessons.title: Understanding the Fenwick lowbit trick
lessons.summary: Bitwise AND of a positive index and its negation extracts its lowest set bit.
lessons.body:
Here n is the number of input elements. Fenwick positions start at 1; the empty prefix is valid, but an update at zero is not. Arithmetic costs assume word-sized values.

## The lowbit trick

The lowest set bit of i is `i & -i` in code. It isolates the rightmost one in the binary representation. In two's-complement arithmetic, negation preserves that bit while flipping the higher bits; AND discards those higher bits. The bit-level derivation is optional:

```formula reference
lowbit(i) = i & (−i)
−i = (~i) + 1
12 = …0000 1100₂
~12 = …1111 0011₂
−12 = …1111 0100₂
12 & (−12) = …0000 0100₂ = 4
where
i: a positive whole number, a position in the tree
lowbit(i): the value of the lowest (rightmost) 1-bit of i
~i: bitwise NOT: i with every bit flipped
&: bitwise AND: a bit is 1 in the result only where it is 1 in both inputs
₂: the number is written in binary (base 2)
…: the same digit repeats to the left (all 0s for a positive number, all 1s for a negative one)
In words: negating a positive index preserves its lowest set bit and flips all higher bits, so AND with the original index keeps just that lowest bit.
```

So `lowbit(12)` is 4: 12 is 1100 in binary, and its rightmost 1 is worth 4. For any odd number the answer is 1.

Python integers behave as if they had infinitely many sign bits, so `i & -i` works there too.

Each entry therefore covers this block:

Entry `t[i]` stores a block ending at position `i`, with length `i & -i`. At index six the block length is two, so the entry covers positions five and six, not the whole prefix.

For an eight-element array:

| i | binary | lowbit | t[i] covers |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0001 | 1 | a[1] |
| 2 | 0010 | 2 | a[1..2] |
| 3 | 0011 | 1 | a[3] |
| 4 | 0100 | 4 | a[1..4] |
| 5 | 0101 | 1 | a[5] |
| 6 | 0110 | 2 | a[5..6] |
| 7 | 0111 | 1 | a[7] |
| 8 | 1000 | 8 | a[1..8] |

Odd indices hold single elements; powers of two hold whole prefixes.

## Key takeaways

- Bitwise AND of a positive index and its negation extracts its lowest set bit.
- Each tree entry stores the block of that length ending at its index.

## Further reading
- [Fenwick trees — cp-algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/fenwick.html)

lessons.title: Fenwick query and update walks
lessons.summary: Queries remove the lowest set bit to move to an earlier block.
lessons.body:
Here n is the number of input elements. Fenwick positions start at 1; the empty prefix is valid, but an update at zero is not. Arithmetic costs assume word-sized values.

## The code

Assume n (the array length) is zero or more, update positions and ranges are valid 1-based positions, and a prefix query asks for anything from 0 to n elements. `add(n + 1, delta)` is an intentional no-op used by range-update boundaries. Complexity counts constant-time word arithmetic; arbitrary-size integer arithmetic has additional bit costs.

```python
class Fenwick:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        # 1-indexed
        self.t = [0] * (n + 1)

    def add(self, i, delta):
        # a[i] += delta
        while i <= self.n:
            self.t[i] += delta
            # Jump to the next enclosing
            # block.
            i += i & -i

    def prefix(self, i):
        # a[1] + ... + a[i]
        s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += self.t[i]
            # Remove this block from the
            # prefix.
            i -= i & -i
        return s

    def range_sum(self, l, r):
        return (self.prefix(r)
                - self.prefix(l - 1))
```

### Querying: strip the lowest bit

`prefix(i)` adds `t[i]`, then removes i's lowest bit to jump to the end of the previous block, and repeats until i is 0:

A query through position thirteen reads entries 13, 12 and 8. Those hold positions 13, 9–12 and 1–8: disjoint blocks covering exactly the requested prefix.

In binary the walk clears the lowest set bit at each step: the prefixes visit indices thirteen, twelve, eight and then zero. The earlier block-count bound shows this is logarithmic in the array length.

### Updating: add the lowest bit

`add(i, delta)` must change every block that contains position i. Those are `t[i]`, then `t[i + lowbit(i)]`, and so on: adding the lowest bit jumps to the next larger block that also covers i.

For a tree of sixteen elements, updating position five visits indices 5, 6, 8 and 16. The next jump reaches 32, outside the tree, so the loop stops.

So `add(5, d)`, with d the value added, changes `t[5]` (element 5), `t[6]` (elements 5 to 6), `t[8]` (elements 1 to 8) and `t[16]` (elements 1 to 16). Each step moves the lowest set bit at least one place left, so this is also O(log n): the number of steps grows with the logarithm of the array length n.

> [!warning] Fenwick trees are 1-indexed
> Index 0 has lowbit 0, so `i += i & -i` would loop forever on `add(0, ...)`. Store `a[k]` at `k + 1` if your data is 0-indexed, and do the shift in one place.

## Key takeaways

- Queries remove the lowest set bit to move to an earlier block.
- Updates add the lowest set bit to visit enclosing blocks; index zero is invalid for updates.
