lessons.title: Indexing text with weighted ropes
lessons.summary: Rope leaves hold chunks; internal weights count left-subtree characters.
lessons.body:
Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations.

## Ropes

Inserting into a single flat text buffer can copy or shift a large part of a 100 MB document. The amount depends on the representation and edit position. A **rope** (Boehm, Atkinson and Plass, 1995) stores the text as a binary tree whose leaves hold short string chunks. Each internal node stores a **rope weight**: the total length of its left subtree.

```
            (9)
          /     \
       (6)       (2)
      /   \     /   \
 "Hello_" "my_" "na" "me_is_Simon"

text: Hello_my_name_is_Simon
```

### Indexing

To find character i, compare it with the weight: go left if smaller, otherwise subtract the weight and go right.

```python
class Leaf:
    def __init__(self, s):
        self.s = s
        self.length = len(s)

class Concat:
    def __init__(self, left, right):
        self.left = left
        self.right = right
        self.weight = left.length
        self.length = (left.length
                       + right.length)

def char_at(node, i):
    if not 0 <= i < node.length:
        raise IndexError(i)
    while isinstance(node, Concat):
        if i < node.weight:
            node = node.left
        else:
            # Skip all characters in the
            # left branch.
            i -= node.weight
            node = node.right
    return node.s[i]
```

For character ten, the root's left subtree contains nine characters, so go right with index one. The right child's left chunk, `na`, has two characters, so go left and read its character one: `a`.

The weights translate a whole-document position into a position relative to the current subtree. Each right descent subtracts exactly the skipped left-subtree length. With balanced, bounded-size chunks, navigation takes O(log n) for n characters; the unbalanced example class itself does not enforce that guarantee.

## Key takeaways

- Rope leaves hold chunks; internal weights count left-subtree characters.
- A right descent subtracts the skipped left-subtree length from the index.

## Further reading
- [SGI rope implementation overview](https://stlab.adobe.com/stldoc_ropeimpl.html)
- [VS Code text-buffer implementation](https://code.visualstudio.com/blogs/2018/03/23/text-buffer-reimplementation)

questions.prompt: Using the rope from the lesson (root weight 9; left child has leaves `Hello_` and `my_` with weight 6; right child has leaves `na` and `me_is_Simon` with weight 2), what does `char_at(root, 15)` return?

options.explanation: That is character 14. Check the subtraction at each step: 15 − 9 = 6, then 6 − 2 = 4, and index 4 of `me_is_Simon` is `s`.
Correct. 15 is at least 9, so go right with index 6; 6 is at least 2, so go right with index 4; `me_is_Simon`[4] is `s`.
This lands in `my_` by going left at the root. Go left only when the index is less than the weight.

options.text: An index error, because no leaf has 15 characters
options.explanation: Leaf lengths don't need to cover the index directly; the weights translate the overall position into a position inside the chunk.

questions.workedExample: The root skips nine left-subtree characters, leaving index six in its right subtree. That subtree skips the two characters in na, leaving index four in me_is_Simon. Character four there is s. Each weight translates a document-wide position into the index within the chosen child; a leaf does not need to contain the original document position.

lessons.title: Rope edits, balancing and practical trade-offs
lessons.summary: Split and concatenate around edits while maintaining balance.
lessons.body:
Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations.

### Operations

Here n is the length of the text in characters and m the number of characters inserted:

| Operation | Flat string | Balanced rope |
|---|---|---|
| Index | O(1) | O(log n) |
| Concatenate | O(n) | O(log n) |
| Insert m new characters | O(n + m) | O(log n + m) |
| Delete a range | O(n) | Implementation-dependent |
| Iterate all | O(n) | O(n) |

These bounds assume balanced trees and bounded leaf sizes, and constant-time character indexing in the flat representation. UTF-8 byte offsets and Unicode character positions need additional care. Inserting new text must read/copy its m characters; deletion can also incur work to reclaim removed nodes. Concatenation creates a new root over two ropes, then rebalances. Insert is split at the position, then two concatenations. Immutable rope nodes can share unchanged structure between versions, making saved-version storage proportional to changed paths plus inserted text. Retaining roots keeps that shared storage alive.

### Real-world use

- Editors: the Xi editor and Zed use rope-like B-trees of text chunks. VS Code instead uses a **piece table** stored in a red–black tree (the "piece tree"), which records edits as references into the original file and an append-only buffer. Both avoid copying the document on each keystroke.
- Libraries: the SGI STL shipped `rope`, and Rust crates such as `ropey` provide them.

Ropes are not always better. For short strings, pointer overhead and lost cache locality can outweigh the editing benefit. Chunking keeps substantial work on contiguous memory; chunk sizes are implementation and workload choices, rather than a universal recommendation.

## Shared-node and balancing pitfalls

- Mutating a "persistent" node: one in-place write corrupts every version sharing that node. Persistence relies on discipline or immutable types.
- **Unbalanced ropes**: repeated appends without rebalancing make a chain with O(n) indexing, where n is the number of leaves.

## Key takeaways

- Split and concatenate around edits while maintaining balance.
- Read or copy inserted characters and account for reclamation and pointer overhead.

## Further reading
- [SGI rope implementation overview](https://stlab.adobe.com/stldoc_ropeimpl.html)
- [VS Code text-buffer implementation](https://code.visualstudio.com/blogs/2018/03/23/text-buffer-reimplementation)

questions.prompt: Starting with one non-empty leaf, a naive rope implementation appends one character at a time with `root = Concat(root, Leaf(c))` and never rebalances. After 10,000 appends, what does `char_at(root, 0)` cost?

options.text: O(1), because index 0 is the first leaf
options.explanation: The first leaf is at the bottom of the tree: every append made a new root whose left child is the old root.

options.text: O(log n), because ropes are trees
options.explanation: Only balanced ropes give O(log n), where n is the number of characters. Without rebalancing, this sequence builds a left-leaning chain.

options.text: About 10,000 steps, O(n), because the tree is a chain of depth 10,000
options.explanation: Correct. Each append wraps the old root, so the first character is 10,000 left moves from the top. This is why balanced ropes rebalance and batch characters into chunks.

options.text: It fails, because weights overflow
options.explanation: The weights store subtree lengths as Python integers; overflow is not the issue here. Depth is.

questions.workedExample:
1. After append 1: `Concat(Leaf(a), Leaf(b))`.
2. After append 2: `Concat(Concat(a, b), Leaf(c))`, one level deeper on the left.
3. Each append adds one level on the left, so after 10,000 appends the leftmost leaf has depth about 10,000.
4. `char_at(root, 0)` always takes the left branch (0 is less than every positive weight), so it walks about 10,000 nodes: O(n), where n is the number of appends (characters) and O(n) means "grows in proportion to n". A balanced rope with bounded chunks would instead need logarithmic navigation; the exact depth depends on its balancing rules.
5. Fixes: rebalance (for example, by Fibonacci-based depth rules from the original rope paper or B-tree nodes), and batch small appends into larger leaves.
